summary:
Austria's statutory baseline is permissive. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016. LGBT people serve openly in the national armed forces, and transgender service members have been permitted to serve openly since 2014.

Legal gender recognition does not require sex-reassignment surgery. A person may be issued an 'X' indeterminate or absent gender marker, and intersex people may choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation at all. The Constitutional Court ruled in June 2018 that official documents must reflect gender identity accurately; Austria issued its first 'X' passport and 'divers' birth certificate in 2019. The Interior Ministry limited 'divers' registration to applicants holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, which means the non-binary marker remains conditional rather than generally available.

The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and has been amended to broaden 'gender' to include gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been banned since 1 January 2016, and offences committed on that ground are treated as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions perceived as biased on sexual orientation grounds.

Recorded violence remains significant. Austria logged 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police and monitoring data are acknowledged to under-record. Between the two broad categories the direction diverges, with homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined over the reporting year.

The most serious documented attack series involved a neo-Nazi network uncovered in March 2025. Police arrested 15 people aged 14 to 26 after at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured through fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and publicly and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is substantially higher.

Detention is addressed directly in the sources. A Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of 2025 sets out the legal framework governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection in custody. The Justice Ministry answered parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 in May and June 2025 on the official rules for housing transgender people in penal institutions; that answer, in German, is the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained.

Government guidance on day-to-day interaction with the state is improving in one respect: an Ombudsman body issued guidance on gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people during 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Political turbulence is measurable. In the September 2024 national election the far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) took the most votes for the first time since the Second World War, at 29.2%, prompting public concern about the consequences of an FPÖ-led government for LGBTQ people. The ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights, so the election result sits within an established pattern of parliamentary hostility rather than marking a break with it.

Administrative friction during 2025 extended beyond enforcement. A petition for queer sauna time slots in Vienna was rejected, and new Ministry of Education rules restricted outside sex-education providers from entering schools. Neither measure restricts a visitor's legal status, but both indicate that inclusion claims made to public bodies may fail.

Political visibility at the other end of the spectrum is high. After the 2019 election seven National Council politicians were openly gay, Iris Eliisa Rauskala became the first openly LGBT government minister in June 2019, Georg Djundja became the first openly gay mayor in April 2019, and President Alexander Van der Bellen joined the 2019 EuroPride parade in Vienna. Public opinion as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing that nothing is wrong with a same-sex relationship.

The divergence between rising homophobic offences and falling transphobic incidents in the 2025 statistics cautions against reading the aggregate hate-crime total as a proxy for trans-specific risk. The category-level trend and the total move in opposite directions.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been covered by the Equal Treatment Act since 2004. Gender identity and intersex status are not named separately but are treated as covered under 'gender'. By January 2017 every federal state had anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation in the supply of goods and services, with Lower Austria the last to adopt it.

Changing legal gender and name does not require prior sex-reassignment surgery, but the change is conditional on a psychiatric opinion, and public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound on submission of psychiatric opinions. Two specialist societies, the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics, have endorsed puberty blockers for youth experiencing gender dysphoria. Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatment.

Conversion therapy has been contested through both administrative and parliamentary routes. In 2018 the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found offering minors classes teaching that sexual orientation was changeable; the Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review and the association itself was banned in April 2019. Parliament passed a non-binding resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a legal ban on conversion therapy on minors, carried unanimously at the final vote.

Community infrastructure operates openly across Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz, including HOSI Wien (founded 1979), HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, alongside an annual Vienna Gay Pride and Regenbogenparade. Advocacy has continued even where the reported sentiment among many LGBT minorities is that being different is itself a problem, a view sources attribute to Catholic influence.

Historical prosecutions were harsh: lesbianism was criminalised after the Anschluss and courts aligned to Paragraph 175 in 1940. As of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme for those historical convictions had been implemented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two source accounts of legal gender recognition conflict and the conflict is unresolved here. One overview states that legal gender recognition is available without mandatory medical procedures, while another states that the change is conditional on a psychiatric opinion. Which requirement a given applicant will actually face is not settled by the material reviewed.

It is unresolved whether the Interior Ministry's restriction of the 'divers' designation to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality remains in force after the 2019 issuance of the first 'X' passport, or whether the marker has since been opened to non-intersex applicants. No source in the reviewed inventory addresses this.

The 2025 hate-crime figures are described by their own publishers as under-recorded, and no explanation is sourced for the fall in transphobic incidents. Whether the decline reflects fewer incidents, lower reporting, or reclassification of motives is not established.

The July 2019 parliamentary resolution calling for a statutory ban on conversion therapy on minors was non-binding, and whether it produced enacted legislation is not sourced. The same gap applies to the status of a general ban covering adults.

The Justice Ministry's answer on housing transgender detainees is available only in German and was not translated for this entry; its specific placement rules, including any provision for self-identification in custody, therefore remain unverified here. Two further pages in the reviewed inventory, covering a regional election and an international human rights organisation's country report, supplied no Austria-specific finding that could be used.
